title: Family and home
goal: Name family members at the right speech level, describe the parts of a house, and use the pointing words *ieu*, *éta*, *itu*.
bekal: family words at both levels, including *lanceuk* and *adi*, which don't mark gender
the parts of a house and the everyday things in it
pointing words for three distances: *ieu*, *éta*, *itu* — English has only two

dialogs.title: Paguneman — Photos on the wall
dialogs.intro: Rani is waiting in Bu Imas's front room, looking at a row of framed photos on the wall. Bu Imas comes in with two glasses of tea.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Keur ningali poto nya? Éta kulawarga Ibu.
lines.id: Looking at the photos? That's my family.
lines.literal: are seeing photos [nya]? that family Ma'am.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Éta carogé Ibu, almarhum. Pupus tilu taun ka tukang.
lines.id: That's my husband, may he rest in peace. He passed away three years ago.
lines.literal: that husband Ma'am, the-late. passed-away three years to back.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Teu nanaon. Ari nu itu, putra Ibu nu cikal, Kang Déni.
lines.id: It's all right. And that one over there is my eldest, Kang Déni.
lines.literal: not anything. as-for which over-there, child Ma'am who eldest, Kang Déni.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Does he live in Bandung too?

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Henteu, di Cirebon. Damel di dinya. Nu bungsu mah di dieu, Néng Sari.
lines.id: No, in Cirebon. He works there. My youngest is right here — Néng Sari.
lines.literal: no, in Cirebon. works at there. who youngest [mah] at here, Néng Sari.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Ooh, Néng Sari téh putra Ibu? Sangka abdi mah anak kos.
lines.id: Oh, Néng Sari is your daughter? I thought she was a lodger.
lines.literal: ooh, Néng Sari [téh] child Ma'am? thought I [mah] child lodging.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Hahaha, seueur nu nyangka kitu. Ari Néng, sabaraha dulur?
lines.id: Hahaha, lots of people think that. What about you, Néng — how many siblings?
lines.literal: hahaha, many who thought like-that. as-for Néng, how-many siblings?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Abdi dua. Aya lanceuk hiji, pameget.
lines.id: There are two of us. I have one older brother.
lines.literal: I two. there-is older-sibling one, male.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Janten Néng téh bungsu. Kolot masih sarerea?
lines.id: So you're the youngest. Are both your parents still living?
lines.literal: so Néng [téh] youngest. parents still all?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Yes, thank God. They're in Bekasi.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Sing sering ditelepon nya. Kolot mah sok ngantosan.
lines.id: Call them often, won't you. Parents are always waiting.
lines.literal: may often phoned [nya]. parents [mah] tend wait.

notes: **Lanceuk** = older sibling, **adi** = younger sibling. Note that **neither** marks male or female. When you need to, add **pameget** (male, lemes) / **istri** (female, lemes), or **lalaki** / **awéwé** in loma. So *lanceuk pameget* = older brother.

**Carogé** = husband (lemes); loma: **salaki**. **Bojo / garwa** = wife (lemes); loma: **pamajikan**. ⚠️ In Javanese *bojo* means wife (or husband); in Sundanese it can mean spouse in general — context decides.

**Pupus** = to pass away (lemes, very respectful). Other forms: *ngantunkeun* (to leave us), *tilar dunya* (to leave the world). ⚠️ Never use **paéh** for people — it is the word for animals and things, and sounds very harsh.
**Cikal** = eldest child, **bungsu** = youngest child, **panengah** = middle child. All three are often used as nouns: *nu cikal* = the eldest.

**Ari** opens a sentence with the sense of "as for", "what about", "whereas". It shifts the conversation to a new topic: *Ari Néng, sabaraha dulur?* = "what about you, Néng — how many siblings?" It is very frequent and very Sundanese; English usually says "what about…" or nothing at all.
**Sangka / nyangka** = to think, assume (wrongly). *Sangka abdi mah…* = "I thought…". The order can also be *abdi nyangka…*

**Sok** here means "tends to, usually", marking a habit: *kolot mah sok ngantosan* = "parents usually wait". ⚠️ Don't confuse it with Indonesian *sok* (show-offy). Its third meaning: *sok atuh* = go ahead, please.

grammars.title: Three distances: ieu, éta, itu
body: English has two pointing words: *this* and *that*. Sundanese has **three**, separated by clear distances.
after: The place words follow the same pattern: **dieu** (here), **dinya** (there, near you), **ditu** (over there, far). For direction: **kadieu** (to here), **kadinya** (to there), **kaditu** (to over there). For origin: **ti dieu**, **ti dinya**, **ti ditu** (from here / there / over there).

⚠️ Sundanese **itu** is **not** a straight translation of "that" (nor of Indonesian *itu*, which works like English "that"). Asking *itu naon?* will be understood, but it means "what's that thing way over there?". For something in the other person's hand, the right question is **éta naon?**
The word **nu** (the one, which) often comes in front to point at things: *nu ieu* (this one), *nu éta* (that one), *nu itu* (the one over there). This is the form you hear most at the market.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Uwa** needs explaining because English has no single word for it: it means an older sibling of your father or mother — male or female. A parent's younger brother is *mamang*, a younger sister *bibi*. So birth order decides the word, not just the blood relation.

blocks.title: Asking about family
items: **Sabaraha dulur?** — How many siblings are there in your family?
**Anak ka sabaraha?** — Where are you in the birth order?
**Tos kagungan putra?** — Do you have children? (lemes, to someone you respect)
**Kolot masih sarerea?** — Are both your parents still living?
**Bumina di mana?** — Where is your house? (to someone you respect)
**Saha jenenganana?** — What is his/her name? (very polite)

sections.title: The house and what's in it

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Ka cai** literally means "to the water" and is the most polite way to say "I need the bathroom" — like "I'll just pop out the back". *Punten, badé ka cai heula.* Saying *jamban* or *WC* outright feels too blunt in someone's front room.

blocks.title: Everyday sentences at home
items: **Panto na dikonci teu?** — Is the door locked?
**Lampu na pareum.** — The light is off. (*hurung* = on)
**Aya cai teu?** — Is there any water?
**Mangga calik di tepas.** — Please have a seat on the porch.
**Punten, badé ka cai heula.** — Excuse me, I just need the bathroom.
**Imahna caket ka dieu.** — The house is close to here. (*caket* = near, *tebih* = far)
